chapters.title: Chapter 2: Measuring Trend - Moving Averages and Crossovers

lessons.title: Case Study: Backtesting a 50-Day/200-Day Crossover on an NSE Stock

children.text: Time to run the filtered crossover rule from Lesson 3 against an actual multi-year stock history and see what it would have produced. Tata Motors is a useful stock for exactly this exercise: a genuine multi-year decline into the 2020 crash, a violent recovery, a rough patch in the 2022 correction, and a sustained rally to fresh highs by 2024. Few NSE large caps pack this many distinct trend regimes, discussed as a general market pattern in Chapter 1's case study, into one stock's own history.

body.text: A single backtest on a single stock is not proof that a strategy works. It is a concrete, worked example of what the mechanics actually produce, trade by trade, including the parts that cost time or money, which is the only way to build real intuition before moving to a more rigorous, multi-stock test.

body.title: Tata Motors: an illustrative price path, 2019-2024 (approximate, rounded)

children.text: Trade Log: What the Filtered Rule Would Have Done
Applying the long-or-flat version of the filtered 50-day/200-day rule from Lesson 3 to this price path produces four position segments.

body.caption: Illustrative trade log, Feb 2019 to end 2024 (illustrative figures, not an actual computed backtest)

cells: Death cross in Feb 2019 kept the strategy out of the entire 2020 crash, buy-and-hold would have been down roughly 59% here
Captured most of the 2021 rally, then gave back some gains during the 2022 correction before the death cross exited
A brief whipsaw: a fresh golden cross re-confirmed just 4 months later, roughly flat over the gap
Captured the bulk of the 2023-2024 rally, position still open at the end of this backtest window

body.text: Because this is a long-or-flat system, not the stop-and-reverse version from Lesson 3, the Jun-Oct 2022 whipsaw cost no capital, only the opportunity cost of sitting out for four months. A stop-and-reverse version of the same rule would have taken an actual short position here instead of going to cash, and a loss on that short leg would show up as a real, capital-losing whipsaw trade rather than a flat one. The choice between the two designs is itself a real risk decision, not just a technical detail.

body.text: Look closely at where the strategy's outperformance actually comes from. Trade 2 and Trade 4 are good trades, but the single biggest contributor is Trade 1: simply not being invested during the 2020 crash. This matches the core, well-documented case for trend following: its real edge is often crash avoidance, not superior stock picking during calm periods.

children.text: What This Backtest Does Not Prove

Tata Motors was chosen for this lesson because its price history happens to illustrate the mechanics clearly, a sustained decline, a crash, and a strong multi-year recovery. That is itself a form of selection bias: picking one stock after already knowing its history flatters almost any trend-following rule tested on it. This backtest also ignores brokerage, STT, and other transaction costs on each entry and exit, ignores slippage between the signal firing and the order actually filling, and rests on only two completed long trades, nowhere near enough to say anything statistically meaningful about the rule's real edge. None of this means the rule is wrong. It means one favorable-looking backtest on one hand-picked stock is a demonstration of mechanics, not evidence of a working strategy. Proper multi-stock, cost-aware backtesting discipline, and the specific traps that make backtests look better than they are, are covered in full later in this course.

body.text: Do not deploy real capital based on a single favorable backtest on a single, already-familiar stock. This case study is a teaching example of how the mechanics from this chapter fit together, not a validated trading strategy.

body.title: Compounding through the two long trades
body.prompt: A ₹1,00,000 position grows by 200% in Trade 2, then, after a flat period with no gain or loss, grows by a further 115.9% in Trade 4. What is the final portfolio value, in rupees?
body.explanation: ₹1,00,000 growing 200% becomes ₹3,00,000 (multiplying by 3). That amount growing a further 115.9% becomes roughly ₹3,00,000 x 2.159 = ₹6,47,700. This is exactly how the strategy's +547.7% total return in the statGrid above was built: multiplying through each trade's return, not adding them.

body.title: Would you trust this result?
body.scenario: A friend shows you this exact backtest and says: "547% returns versus 179% for buy-and-hold, this crossover rule clearly works, I'm deploying it on my full portfolio next week."
body.prompt: Based on this lesson, what would you say to your friend before they deploy real capital?
body.modelAnswer: The result is a real demonstration of how the mechanics work, but it rests on a single, already-familiar stock chosen partly because its history flatters the strategy, only two completed long trades, and no accounting for transaction costs, slippage, or taxes. Before deploying real capital, your friend should test the same rule across a broad basket of NSE stocks, not just one, check whether the result holds up after realistic costs, and see whether the parameters chosen, the 50-day and 200-day windows, the 1% band, the 20-day slope lookback, were tuned with the benefit of hindsight on this exact stock's history. One good-looking backtest on a hand-picked example is a starting point for further testing, not a green light to size up and deploy immediately.

cards.definition: The largest peak-to-trough decline in a portfolio's or strategy's value over a given period, a key measure of how much pain a strategy can inflict along the way.
Valuing a still-open position at its current market price to measure unrealized gain or loss, as opposed to a closed trade's realized return.
The distortion that results from testing a strategy on an example chosen because its outcome is already known, which tends to flatter the strategy's apparent performance.
A trend-following strategy's tendency to exit or avoid an asset during a severe decline, often the single largest source of its outperformance versus buy-and-hold.

points: Applying the filtered crossover rule from Lesson 3 to Tata Motors' 2019-2024 price path produces four position segments: flat, long, flat, long, illustrating the mechanics from the whole chapter in one worked example.

In this illustrative backtest, the strategy's headline outperformance versus buy-and-hold comes mostly from avoiding the 2020 crash entirely, not from superior trades during calmer periods, consistent with trend following's well-documented real-world case.
Because the system is long-or-flat rather than stop-and-reverse, its one whipsaw cost time, not capital, a design choice worth weighing deliberately.

A single backtest on one hand-picked, already-familiar stock demonstrates mechanics, it does not validate a strategy, given selection bias, ignored transaction costs, and a tiny sample of completed trades.
Rigorous multi-stock, cost-aware backtesting, and the specific traps that make results like this one look better than they really are, are covered in full later in this course.
